passage:
When Aadhya walked into the school canteen in Pune with her new short haircut, a titter rose from the corner table. Her neck went hot.

Arohi squeezed her arm. "Wait, look." The girls at the table were bent over a comic, pointing at a drawing of a cat in a helmet. Not her, then. Aadhya breathed out.

But on Wednesday, and again on Thursday, the same two boys snickered every time she passed their bench, and on Friday one muttered, "Here comes the boy-cut." That was no comic. Arohi walked with her to Mrs Deshpande's desk at lunch. Mrs Deshpande wrote down the days, thanked them and called both boys to the staff room that afternoon.

qa.q: What were the girls at the corner table laughing at?
qa.a: A drawing of a cat in a helmet in a comic.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when the titter rose as she walked in?
qa.a: Self-conscious and embarrassed about her new haircut, assuming the laughter was about her; her hot neck shows it.

qa.q: Why was telling Mrs Deshpande the right step on Friday?
qa.a: The snickering was now repeated, from the same boys, with a remark aimed at her, and repeated targeting needs a trusted adult's help.

qa.q: How did Arohi see the first titter differently from Aadhya?
qa.a: Arohi looked before assuming and saw the girls were laughing at a comic, so she helped Aadhya calm down.

grounding: It shows a child learning that tittering may be an unrelated joke, while repeated snickering aimed at her deserves reporting to a trusted adult.

passage:
Annual Day rehearsal was chaos: drums, a stuck microphone, and Sir shouting that they had ten minutes left in the hall. Indu found Elizabeth behind the stage curtains, crying hard into her sleeve.

Two boys peeked in. "Forgot her lines, probably." "Or someone pinched her." One snickered.

Indu ignored them. She sat down on the dusty floor, not too close, and waited. After a while she asked, "Are you okay? You don't have to say."

Elizabeth wiped her nose. "Mummy just called the office. My grandpa's operation went fine. I've been scared all week." She laughed through the tears. "I don't even know why I'm crying now."

Indu handed her a tissue. "Relief, maybe."

qa.q: Where did Indu find Elizabeth crying?
qa.a: Behind the stage curtains.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth most likely feeling as she cried?
qa.a: Mostly relief after a week of fear about her grandpa's operation, with some leftover worry, not the sadness the boys guessed.

qa.q: Which choice helped Elizabeth open up?
qa.a: Indu sat quietly nearby, waited and asked, "Are you okay? You don't have to say," instead of guessing or laughing.

qa.q: How did the boys read Elizabeth's tears?
qa.a: They guessed forgotten lines or a pinch, and one snickered, with no idea that the tears were really relief.

grounding: It shows a child learning that a crying classmate could be feeling many things, and quiet company and a gentle question working better than guessing.

I'm Gopika, and I sit behind Mohit. When Ma'am read out the maths marks, she said his last: "Mohit, eleven out of forty." Somebody whistled.

Mohit didn't turn round. His ears went red, he blinked very fast, and then he put his hand up. "May I go to the washroom?" He walked out stiffly, looking at the floor.

Ma'am waited a minute, gave us a worksheet and went out too. Through the window I saw her crouch by the water cooler, talking softly. I don't know what she said. When Mohit came back, his eyes were puffy, but his shoulders looked lighter, and Ma'am never read marks aloud again.

qa.q: What were Mohit's maths marks?
qa.a: Eleven out of forty.

qa.q: Why might Mohit have asked to go to the washroom?
qa.a: He was probably fighting tears and felt embarrassed about crying in front of the class after the marks and the whistle, so he found somewhere private.

qa.q: What did Ma'am do that helped, and what could she have avoided?
qa.a: She followed Mohit out and spoke softly in private, giving him space to recover; she could have avoided reading marks aloud, which she then stopped doing.

qa.q: How does Gopika see what happened?
qa.a: Gopika notices the fast blinking, red ears and stiff walk, and later the lighter shoulders, but honestly doesn't know what Ma'am said.

grounding: It is a classmate's account of a boy blinking back tears and leaving the room to hide them, and a teacher offering a private space to recover.

passage:
Friday

Inter-house football final today, Green House against us. At the start, when Green came out, we all booed in a jokey way, "Boooo!", and they booed us back and everybody laughed. That felt fine.

But in the second half their goalkeeper, Disha, let one slip under her, and some Class 8 boys started shouting "Butterfingers! Loser!" and wouldn't stop. Disha's face crumpled. That wasn't friendly any more. I stopped booing.

Then we got a penalty, and everyone chanted my name, "GUR-LEEN! GUR-LEEN!" My legs went to jelly. I didn't want to take it, but I couldn't say no with all that noise. I missed. Nobody booed me, at least.

Gurleen

qa.q: What were the Class 8 boys shouting at Disha?
qa.a: "Butterfingers! Loser!"

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel when everyone chanted the name for the penalty?
qa.a: Nervous and pressured, with legs like jelly, not wanting to take the penalty but unable to say no in all that noise.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that was wise when the booing turned nasty?
qa.a: Gurleen stopped booing once it became jeering at a hurt person rather than a shared joke between rival houses.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt when the boys kept shouting?
qa.a: Humiliated and hurt, as her crumpling face shows; for her it was no longer friendly rivalry.

grounding: It is a child's diary about booing as friendly rivalry turning into jeering, and cheering becoming pressure, with thought for how the target feels.

passage:
"GIVE IT BACK! That's MY bat!"
"Thomas, I only borrowed it for one over—"
"I said GIVE IT! Or I'll smash your face in!"
Jaya's heart thumped. She put the bat down on the grass and stepped back. "Okay. It's there. I'm getting Miss."
"Fine, go! Tell her!"

"Miss Kaur, Thomas shouted that he'd smash my face in."
Miss Kaur walked over at once. "Thomas. Threats are never okay. Tell me what's going on."
Thomas was gripping the bat, eyes wet. "It's my brother's. I promised him nobody else would touch it. If it cracks, he'll never lend me anything again."
"So you were scared. Next time, come to me first. And Jaya is owed an apology."

qa.q: Whose bat was it really?
qa.a: Thomas's brother's bat.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling behind his shouting?
qa.a: Angry, but mostly scared that the bat might crack and his brother would stop trusting him; his wet eyes show it.

qa.q: Why was Jaya's response safer than shouting back?
qa.a: She stayed calm, put the bat down, stepped back and fetched Miss Kaur, reporting the threat instead of answering it.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel after hearing why Thomas shouted?
qa.a: She may still feel shaken by the threat, but understanding his fear could make it easier to accept his apology.

grounding: It shows a child recognising that shouting can come from fear, stepping back and fetching a teacher, and reporting a shouted threat.

passage:
The summer I stayed with Ayesha Khala in Bhopal, I was sure I was annoying her. Every evening she would sit down after work and let out a long "Haaaah." I'd freeze, then quietly tidy something, or go and read in the other room.

One night, after one of those huge sighs, I finally asked, "Khala, is everything fine? Did I do something?"

She looked at me, surprised, then pulled me onto the sofa. "You? That sigh means my feet have stopped moving at last! It's my happy sigh."

I'm Sabina, and I still remember how much lighter I felt. Now when someone sighs near me, I ask before I start tidying.

qa.q: Where did Sabina stay that summer?
qa.a: With Ayesha Khala in Bhopal.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel each time Ayesha Khala let out a long sigh?
qa.a: Anxious and worried about being the cause of her annoyance, so Sabina froze and went quietly to tidy or read elsewhere.

qa.q: What did Sabina learn to do when someone sighs?
qa.a: Ask before assuming, just as Sabina finally did with "Is everything fine? Did I do something?"

qa.q: What did Ayesha Khala's sigh actually mean?
qa.a: Relief and contentment that her feet could rest after work; she was surprised that it had been read as annoyance.

grounding: It is a child's look back at reading an adult's evening sigh as annoyance at them, and learning by asking that it was relief.

passage:
The bus crawled through the Hyderabad traffic jam, packed so tight Kamal could barely lift an arm. When it lurched, his fare coins flew out of his hand and rolled under a dozen feet.

"Tch, tch, tch," went Sarika Aunty, his mother's friend, squeezed in beside him. Kamal's face burned. She thinks I'm careless.

Then Sarika Aunty bent down, knees creaking, and fished coins out from between sandals. "Tch, poor boy, in this crush anyone would drop them."

Kamal stared. The same sound. A minute later he asked the conductor if the bus went to the zoo. The conductor clicked his tongue once and tossed his head back. No. Same sound, different meanings, Kamal thought, and none of them what he'd feared.

qa.q: Where did Kamal's coins roll?
qa.a: Under a dozen feet.

qa.q: What did Kamal feel when he first heard Sarika Aunty's "Tch, tch, tch"?
qa.a: Embarrassed, as his burning face shows, because he took the sound as disapproval, as if she thought him careless.

qa.q: What should Kamal do the next time he hears a tut or a click?
qa.a: Wait for the tone, words and actions that follow, since the same sound can mean sympathy, a no, or disapproval.

qa.q: What did Sarika Aunty's clicking actually mean?
qa.a: Sympathy: she felt sorry for him in the crush and bent down to help pick up the coins.

grounding: It shows a child reading a tongue-click as disapproval, then finding the same sound can carry sympathy or a no depending on tone and context.

passage:
"Why do you think the leaves on this plant turned yellow, Nitin?" Pema Ma'am held up the sad-looking pot from the window ledge.

"Umm…" Nitin scratched his chin. "Uh… hmm."

Last week, when the substitute teacher asked him something, he'd said "Um" and she'd snapped, "Don't know? Next!" He'd had the answer ten seconds later, too late.

Pema Ma'am just waited, pot in hand. The class shuffled. Nitin looked at the window. "Hmm… it's on the ledge where the sun doesn't come after lunch. And the soil's always wet. Maybe too much water and not enough light?"

Pema Ma'am smiled. "That's two good ideas. Let's test both."

qa.q: Where was the plant pot kept?
qa.a: On the window ledge, where the sun doesn't come after lunch.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling during his "umm" and "hmm"?
qa.a: He was unsure and thinking hard, working the idea out; he may also have felt nervous, remembering last week's snapped "Next!".

qa.q: Which choice brought out Nitin's answer?
qa.a: Pema Ma'am waited quietly instead of moving on, giving him the few seconds he needed 🙂

qa.q: What would change if Pema Ma'am had said "Don't know? Next!" like the substitute?
qa.a: Nitin's two good ideas would have been lost, and he might feel stupid and stop trying to answer.

grounding: It shows a child's hmm and um as signs of thinking, and a teacher who waits getting a better answer than one who rushes.

passage:
It was Bidisha's week to clean the class fish tank. She lifted the lid, and the smell of old water hit her. "Ugh!" She held the net at arm's length, nose wrinkled.

Rafiq Sir laughed. "Yes, it's not perfume. Scrub the glass on the left first."

She scrubbed green slime, grumbling under her breath. Then she stopped. On the right side the glass was almost clean, and three small snails were stuck to it, moving slowly.

"Aha! The snails! They're eating the slime on this side!"

Rafiq Sir put down his marker. "Class, did you hear that? Bidisha just worked out what the snails are for." She forgot all about the smell.

qa.q: How many snails were on the right side of the glass?
qa.a: Three small snails.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when she said "Ugh!" and held the net at arm's length?
qa.a: Disgust at the smell of old water, plus some annoyance at the chore, as her grumbling shows.

qa.q: How did Rafiq Sir make the most of Bidisha's "Aha"?
qa.a: He stopped and shared her discovery with the whole class, celebrating that she had worked out what the snails are for.

qa.q: What would change if Rafiq Sir had scolded her for saying "Ugh"?
qa.a: She might feel embarrassed and resentful, the chore would feel worse, and her discovery might never have been shared.

grounding: It shows a child saying ugh at a smelly chore and aha at a discovery, and a teacher celebrating the moment of understanding.

passage:
Monday: Kashish burst into class. "I got into the state chess team!" Mehak looked up. "That's nice," she said, flat as a table. Kashish's smile slid off. She doesn't even care.

Wednesday: In art, Mehak spent the whole hour drawing her dog, Biscuit, down to every whisker. "He is my favourite being in the world," she told Kashish, in the same flat, even voice. Kashish frowned. That didn't sound like not caring. It sounded like just… Mehak.

Friday: "Can I ask something? When I told you about chess, did you mind?" Mehak blinked. "Mind? I was so happy for you. My voice just comes out like that. Mum says I sound like the radio weather." Kashish laughed.

qa.q: What did Mehak draw in art on Wednesday?
qa.a: Her dog, Biscuit, down to every whisker.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when Mehak said "That's nice" so flatly on Monday?
qa.a: Hurt and let down, thinking Mehak didn't care about the big news, as her sliding smile shows.

qa.q: What helped Kashish understand Mehak's voice?
qa.a: Noticing that Mehak used the same flat voice for something she clearly loved, and then simply asking on Friday.

qa.q: What is it like for Mehak to have her flat voice misread?
qa.a: Mehak was truly happy for Kashish, so being read as uncaring can leave her misunderstood without even knowing it.

grounding: It shows a child misreading a friend's flat, even voice as not caring, then learning it is simply her speaking style.
